title: Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
summary: This sub-technique is the credential focused branch of victim identity gathering, and it is the one that most directly enables access. Credentials reach an adversary by three main routes. The first is harvesting, where the attacker collects the secret from the victim, often through a login page that proxies the real one so the victim completes a genuine multi-factor authentication challenge and the attacker keeps the resulting session. The second is markets, where infostealer logs containing browser saved usernames and passwords are sold in bulk through criminal shops and messaging channels. The third is exposure, where credentials sit in breach datasets, public code repositories, configuration files, or search engine results. A related behaviour is targeting an identity or communication provider so that one time codes forwarded through that service can be intercepted. The important defensive idea is that a leaked password list is only dangerous when it matches a live account, which makes password reuse and weak reset processes the real problem. On the telemetry side the useful artefacts are authentication logs and identity provider records: failed sign in bursts across many accounts, successful sign ins from new locations or unusual clients, token replay indicators where no new authentication challenge occurred, and multi-factor authentication method changes made shortly after a suspicious sign in.

beginner.definition: Credentials are the usernames and passwords that prove who you are. This technique is about attackers collecting the credentials of people in a target company. They want them so they can sign in as a real employee.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen password can skip the hard work of breaking in. If you reuse one password, a leak from a shopping site can open your work account. Attackers also buy stolen password lists cheaply, so a single mistake can be found and used months later.
howItWorks: The attacker builds a fake sign in page that looks exactly like the real one.
The victim types their password and approves the real security prompt, which the attacker captures.
Alternatively the attacker simply buys stolen password logs from online criminal shops.
They then test the collected credentials against the target's own sign in service.
A match gives them access as that user, sometimes without any new security prompt.
The identity logs then show failed attempts, new locations, and changed security settings.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where one key opens the front door, the bike shed, and the storeroom. If a copy of that key is lost at the market, it does not matter which lock it came from, because it opens everything. That is why one reused password can put your work account at risk.
takeaways: One reused password can turn an unrelated breach into your problem.
Session records can be stolen, so a login can happen without a new password prompt.
Watch for many failed sign ins followed by one success from a new location.

objectives: Define credentials and explain why they are valuable during reconnaissance.
Describe how credential harvesting pages capture a password and a session.
Explain how infostealer logs and breach datasets bring credentials to market.
Identify the identity logs that reveal credential misuse after a leak.
Explain why password reuse and session theft complicate multi-factor authentication.
